questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A technical report read against a claim
questions.learningObjective: Identify which findings in a technical report bear on the date of an object
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet for the smoked duck crown lists a twelve percent discount for the carved oak panel above the pass, and a technical report claims the panel is sixteenth century. Which point in the report would most directly test that claim?

options.text: A dendrochronology range of 1490 to 1520, which dates the felling of the wood rather than the carving
A note that the panel was varnished in 1780, which shows only when the varnish was applied
options.misconception: mistakes a later varnish date for the date of the carving

options.text: A line reporting that the panel was cleaned in 2019, which bears on condition and not on age
options.misconception: treats a conservation record as evidence of original age

options.text: An estimate that the panel is worth more than the dinner service, which is a question of price
options.misconception: reads market value as though it were proof of age

questions.explanation: Dendrochronology dates the felling of the timber, so it can bracket the panel and test the claim directly. A varnish date, a cleaning date and a price estimate all sit outside the question of when the object was made.
questions.hint: Ask which evidence bears on when the object was made.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The two sides of a disputed attribution
questions.learningObjective: Compare two competing lists of evidence and state the size of the gap between them
questions.stem: On the costing sheet for a venison course, an inlaid cabinet is priced at 2,400 once a disputed attribution is settled. One side of the dispute cites nine traits as typical of the earlier workshop, the other cites five traits that are atypical. How many more traits does the first side cite?

options.text: Four more traits, because nine typical traits minus five atypical traits leaves four
Fourteen traits in all, because nine traits plus five traits sums to fourteen
options.misconception: adds the two sides together instead of comparing them

options.text: Two more traits, because nine traits divided by five traits rounds down to one
options.misconception: divides one count by the other instead of subtracting

options.text: Five more traits, because the smaller count is read as a surplus over zero
options.misconception: reads the smaller count as a surplus rather than a difference

questions.explanation: The question asks for the gap between the two lists, so nine less five gives four. Adding the lists, dividing them, or reading the smaller figure as a surplus all answer a different question about the evidence.
questions.hint: Compare the two lists rather than combining them.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Weighing evidence in a disputed attribution
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes one side of a disputed attribution stronger than the other
questions.stem: A nine percent discount is applied on a chef's recipe costing sheet to a brass-mounted casket only if the report weighing the disputed attribution comes down for the later workshop. Explain what would make one side of that evidence stronger than the other.

answer.exemplar: A strong side rests on evidence that is contemporary with the object, independent of its later reputation and diagnostic of a particular date, while a weak side rests on features that are widely shared, restorable, or merely typical of a broad period. The decisive test is whether the weaker evidence could be explained away by ordinary workshop practice of the time.

questions.explanation: Weight turns on how specific and how close in time each piece of evidence is. Evidence shared by many workshops cannot separate the two attributions, while a dated record naming the maker or patron can.
questions.hint: Ask which evidence is both close in time and specific.

questions.hint: Subtract the failing samples from the number sampled.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Pastiche distinguished from forgery
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an honest later imitation from a work made to deceive

stimulus.body: A supplier describes a landscape panel as a genuine eighteenth-century work and asks the restaurant to price it accordingly. A second supplier offers a similar panel made in the 1880s by deliberately imitating the earlier style, and priced far below the first.

questions.stem: A supplier's note about a landscape panel sits on the chef's recipe costing sheet, and a second supplier offers a similar panel from the 1880s at a much lower price. Which statement best separates the two panels?

options.text: The 1880s panel is a forgery because its style is old-fashioned, and old-fashioned styling always means deception
options.misconception: equates an old-fashioned style with fraudulent intent

options.text: The 1880s panel is a pastiche because it imitates an earlier style deliberately and is openly of its own date
Both panels are pastiches, since any work that follows an earlier style is a deliberate imitation of it
options.misconception: treats every follower of a style as a deliberate imitator

options.text: Neither panel is a pastiche, because a pastiche may only combine features drawn from two different artists
options.misconception: insists pastiche must mix two artists rather than one earlier period

questions.explanation: Pastiche is honest imitation, a work made in one period in the manner of an earlier one. Forgery depends on passing a work off as older than it is, which the 1880s supplier is not attempting to do.
questions.hint: Ask whether the maker meant the work to be taken for older.

questions.topic: What an unfinished surface shows
questions.learningObjective: Order the report and the pricing decision when the surface is unfinished
questions.stem: A chef's costing sheet lists a spalted oak settle board as a finished sixteenth-century panel, although its underside is bare and gessoed. Which pairing of report step and pricing step is the sounder reading of the evidence?

options.text: Record the unfinished state, then raise the price because rarity makes an unfinished panel more valuable
options.misconception: assumes rarity always raises the price of an unfinished object

options.text: Record the bare underside as proof the panel is a later copy, then price it as a forgery and refuse it
options.misconception: treats an unfinished surface as decisive proof of a later copy

options.text: Record the unfinished state as evidence of the panel's original purpose, then price it as an incomplete work
Raise the price first to cover the work, then record the unfinished state to justify the higher figure
options.misconception: reverses the order, letting the price dictate the finding

questions.explanation: The bare underside and prepared gesso are evidence about how the panel was made and used, so the report states that before a price is set. An unfinished state alone proves neither a copy nor a forgery.
questions.hint: Ask what the surface shows before asking what it costs.

questions.learningObjective: Sequence the stages of a technical examination in the sound order
questions.stem: A saffron risotto line on a chef's recipe costing sheet carries a charger that arrived with a technical report attached. Which sequence best fits the order in which a conservator would normally carry out an examination?

options.text: Imaging first, then a judgement, then reading the results, so the finding can be published quickly
options.misconception: prioritises a quick announcement over sound order

options.text: A judgement about date first, then visual survey, then sampling, so the report can confirm what is expected
options.misconception: assumes the conclusion first and hunts for support

options.text: Sampling first, then a judgement about date, then visual survey, since sampling is the least visible step
options.misconception: believes the least visible step must logically come first

options.text: Visual survey, then sampling and imaging, then reading the results, and only then a judgement about date

questions.explanation: A conservator records what is visible, gathers evidence, reads results, and only then judges the date. Starting with a judgement, or announcing one before the results are read, inverts the sound order.
questions.hint: Ask what the examiner can know before testing anything.

questions.stem: A costing sheet for the honey tart carries a column of panel evidence for a painted cabinet: forty leaves are recorded in total and six of them were repainted in a later campaign. How many leaves are consistent with the earliest campaign?

options.text: Forty-six leaves, because forty recorded leaves plus six repainted leaves gives forty-six
options.misconception: adds the later repainting to the total instead of removing it

options.text: Thirty-four leaves, because forty recorded leaves less six repainted leaves leaves thirty-four
Two hundred and forty leaves, because forty leaves multiplied by six gives two hundred and forty
options.misconception: multiplies the two counts when the question calls for a difference

options.text: Six leaves, because only the repainted leaves carry a campaign that can be dated
options.misconception: counts the later campaign and ignores the earlier one

questions.explanation: Six of the forty recorded leaves belong to a later campaign, so the earliest one accounts for the other thirty-four. Adding, multiplying, or counting only the later campaign answers a different question.
questions.hint: Remove the later campaign from the recorded total.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A technical report read against a claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a later coating must be kept apart from an attribution claim
questions.stem: The report attached to a chef's recipe costing sheet argues that a painted panel is by the later of two hands, and the sheet carries a separate cost line for a coating of old varnish. Explain why that cost line is worth keeping apart from the question of attribution.

answer.exemplar: A varnish line records the cost of a later protective or restorative coating and belongs to the condition and upkeep of the object, not to its authorship. Keeping it separate stops a cheap and often modern coating from being read as evidence of a very early date, and leaves the attribution resting on the paint layer itself, where the question belongs.

questions.explanation: A varnish records a later intervention on the surface, not the hand that made the object. Separating the two stops a cheap modern coating from being read as evidence of great age.
questions.hint: Ask what the coating tells you about the surface, not the hand.

questions.topic: Weighing evidence in a disputed attribution
questions.learningObjective: Record an unsupported attribution claim in a defensible way on a costing sheet

stimulus.body: A gallery statement reproduced in the press says the panel above the restaurant pass is by the later of two hands. The statement is brief and gives no sampling results and no documentary references. The kitchen must decide what to write in the column headed supplier assurance.

questions.stem: A press statement on the chef's recipe costing sheet claims a mural figure is by the later of two hands and offers no supporting detail. Which entry in the sheet's assurance column is defensible?

options.text: Price the mural as a later work, since the statement must be right for the dinner service to go ahead
options.misconception: lets a commercial deadline decide an attribution question

options.text: Record the mural as securely by the later hand, since a published gallery statement carries authority
options.misconception: treats a published claim as though it were a test result

options.text: Record the claim as an unverified supplier statement, with the disputed attribution left open on the sheet
Leave the mural out of the pricing entirely, since no attribution can ever be settled in public
options.misconception: assumes attribution can never be settled by evidence at all

questions.explanation: A published statement is a claim rather than a test, so the sheet can record it while leaving the attribution open. Treating a press notice as a result, or letting service pressure settle it, overreaches.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statement reports a test or makes a claim.

questions.stem: On a chef's recipe costing sheet a carved choir screen is entered at 3,200 with a note that a conservation report is still pending. The report sets out the surface evidence first and the documentary record second. Which reading of that order is correct?

options.text: The order is arbitrary because the two kinds of evidence carry exactly the same weight
options.misconception: claims all evidence weighs the same regardless of its date

options.text: Surface evidence is recorded first because it is cheapest to obtain, and the documents then confirm it
options.misconception: treats the cheapest evidence as automatically the strongest

options.misconception: assumes documents are never revised or misread later

options.text: Surface evidence is recorded first because it is the primary record, and the documentary record then tests it

options.text: The tray was made in the nineteenth century, so it belongs among forgeries because its style is much earlier
options.misconception: confuses a later date with a deceitful intention

options.text: Copying was normal in the decorative trades, and only an intention to deceive separates a copy from a forgery
Pieces made after a famous workshop closed are always forgeries, whatever the buyers were told
options.misconception: assumes a late date alone proves fraudulent intent

questions.hint: Ask what the maker intended the buyer to believe.

options.misconception: subtracts the wrong column and reads the remainder

Sixty-two per cent, because eight attributed panels are divided by thirteen named panels

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of a technical examination
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the sequence of an examination can be read from a report
questions.stem: On the costing sheet for a chilled soup, a note says a painted panel was left unfinished at the gesso stage, and the report gives a reason for the halt. Explain how the order of an examination can be read off a report like this.

answer.exemplar: A sound report moves from what can be seen without intervention, through sampling and analysis, to a judgement about date, and the reason given for halting the work at the gesso stage shows where in that sequence the examination stood. Reading the sequence in that order prevents a provisional observation, such as a prepared ground, being treated as a final conclusion about the object.

questions.explanation: A report that moves from visible survey to analysis and only then judges the date preserves the order of examination. Read another way, a preliminary observation such as a gesso ground is taken for a conclusion.
questions.hint: Look for the stage at which the work stopped and what it rested on.

questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet carries two rival descriptions of a carved screen, neither supported by a document. Which of the two claims needs the stronger documentary case?

options.text: Both claims equally, because two unsupported descriptions balance each other and settle nothing
options.misconception: treats two unsupported claims as a fair weighing of evidence

options.text: The claim that the screen is a later work, because a later work in an old manner is harder to disguise
options.misconception: reverses the burden and treats the later work as the harder case

questions.explanation: The harder claim to sustain is the one needing a positive document, and a celebrated attribution is that claim. Physical evidence can still carry weight, and two unsupported descriptions do not balance into a finding.

options.misconception: prefers what photographs well over what informs the date

options.text: Losses reveal what the original surface was made of, while overpaint can only record what a later hand covered

answer.exemplar: A count of nine matching points out of twelve is strong support for the claimed workshop, because the sampling is direct and the matches are specific, but it is not a proof: three discordant points remain and may themselves be informative. answer.exemplar: An underdrawing records the first working decision of the painter, and its style, the hand behind the contour, and the presence of corrections made before any colour was added are all early evidence that later repainting cannot easily imitate. When such a sketch is contemporary with the panel's preparation, it carries the painter's manner directly, and the period can be fixed from those traits.

questions.explanation: An underdrawing records the painter's first decisions, and its hand, corrections and style are hard to imitate later. When contemporary with the preparation, its traits fix the work within a period.

Both dates equally, since a varnish settles a surface as firmly as an invoice settles a date

questions.stem: A panel in the kitchen's costing file is described as a nineteenth-century copy of an earlier design, and the report says the copy was made for a collector who knew exactly what it was. Explain what this shows about the kind of object it is.

answer.exemplar: Knowing the age of a work changes the meaning of the imitation entirely. A copy commissioned or bought openly by someone who knew the original's date is a deliberate exercise in a recognised style, and it carries no deception, however close the copy comes to the model. The report should therefore record a copy made in a dated tradition, not a forgery or a work built to mislead.

questions.explanation: When the maker and the buyer both knew the age, the imitation carries no deception. A copy made openly for a knowing collector is a deliberate exercise in a style, and the sheet should record it as such.
questions.hint: Ask what the buyer's knowledge removes from the question.

questions.learningObjective: Write an accurate and fair entry for a work made in an earlier manner

stimulus.body: A gallery note describes a painted panel as a pastiche in the manner of an earlier master, made for a collector's cabinet rather than for an altar. The note adds that the panel was never sold as an original and that the collector's inventory records it under the artist's name. The kitchen must decide how the sheet records the object.

questions.stem: A gallery note on the chef's recipe costing sheet calls a panel a pastiche made for a collector's cabinet. Which entry for the sheet is both accurate and fair to the work?

options.text: Record an original by the earlier master, because the inventory names him and the gallery is silent
options.misconception: relies on a heading while ignoring the gallery's own description

options.text: Record a forgery, because the collector's inventory entered it under the earlier master's name
options.misconception: treats a cataloguer's heading as a deceptive sale

options.text: Record a later work in the manner of an earlier master, made openly and not offered as an original
Record a pastiche, because combining the manner of one artist with the taste of another is imitation
options.misconception: defines pastiche as a mixture of two artists, not one earlier style

questions.explanation: The note describes a later work made openly in an earlier manner, which is a pastiche, and an inventory heading is no deception. Neither the heading nor the note makes the panel an original.
questions.hint: Ask whether the work was ever offered as something it is not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an unfinished surface shows
questions.learningObjective: Compare the dating value of a ground and a drawn line on an unfinished surface
questions.stem: A panel on a chef's recipe costing sheet is described as unfinished, and the report notes both the sketch lines and the gilding bole beneath them. Which of the two features gives firmer ground for a date, and what does the other leave open?

options.text: Both equally, because any feature of an unfinished surface dates it as well as another
options.misconception: assumes all features of a surface weigh the same

options.text: The sketch lines, because a drawn contour carries the hand of the maker in a way a ground cannot
options.misconception: rates a drawing as more diagnostic than a workshop's ground

options.text: Neither, because an unfinished surface gives no evidence of date and only of condition
options.misconception: denies that an unfinished surface can bear on date

options.text: The bole, because a gilding ground applied before the drawing shows the order of the workshop's work

questions.explanation: A gilding ground laid before the drawing fixes the order of the workshop's work. A contour is dated by style, which is weaker, and the two features do not weigh equally.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two came first in the making.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of a technical examination
questions.learningObjective: State the principle that makes a sequence of examination steps sound
questions.stem: A conservation report for a hotel's stair panel sets out its examination in numbered steps, and the sheet asks the kitchen to use that order when writing the entry. Which principle of the order matters most for the entry to be sound?

options.text: That the steps can be reordered for presentation, since the reader judges the outcome rather than the process
options.misconception: lets presentation order stand in for the order of analysis

options.text: That each step rests on the step before, so the entry states no conclusion before its evidence
That the cheapest steps come first, so that a short report can be produced under budget
options.misconception: orders analysis by cost rather than by dependence

options.text: That the final step is written first, so that the entry can be summarised from the top
options.misconception: inverts the order so a summary can lead

questions.explanation: A sound sequence builds each step on the results of the one before, so no conclusion appears before its evidence. Reordering for presentation, sorting by cost, or leading with the summary weaken it.
questions.hint: Ask what each step in the sequence depends on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A campaign that the materials contradict
questions.learningObjective: Total the campaign weights recorded in a conservation file
questions.stem: A cost sheet for the dining room lists a cabinet of eighteen leaves, and a report assigns a weight of two to the earliest campaign and a weight of one to the later one. How many campaign weights does the report assign in total?

options.text: Three, because a weight of two for the earliest campaign plus a weight of one for the later gives three
Two, because only the earliest campaign carries a weight in the report
options.misconception: ignores the later campaign when totalling the weights

options.text: One, because a weight of two for the earliest campaign divided by the later weight gives one
options.misconception: divides the two weights instead of summing them

options.text: Nine, because the nine leaves of the earliest campaign are each counted as a weight
options.misconception: counts objects instead of the weights the report assigns

questions.explanation: The report assigns a weight of two and a weight of one, which total three. Counting only the first campaign, dividing the two weights, or counting leaves rather than weights each answer a different question.
questions.hint: Add the two weights the report assigns.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A technical report read against a claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a report means when it calls a claim unsupported
questions.stem: A cost line in a chef's recipe costing sheet prices a panel at 1,000 with a note that the report calls the claim of age unsupported. Explain what a report means when it says a claim is unsupported, and how the sheet should act on that.

answer.exemplar: Unsupported means the evidence brought forward does not yet carry the claim, not that the claim has been proved false. The report should say which tests were made and what they failed to establish, so that the sheet can price the panel on what is actually known, and so that a later test, a clearer document or a fresh opinion can change the entry if the evidence warrants it.

questions.explanation: Unsupported means the evidence does not yet carry the claim, not that the claim is false. The sheet should price on what is known and keep the entry open to a later test or document.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim has been disproved or merely unproved.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The two sides of a disputed attribution
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the leaves belonging to the earliest campaign of a painted cabinet
questions.stem: A conservator's tally for a cabinet on a chef's recipe costing sheet records forty leaves in total, six of which were repainted in a later campaign. How many leaves are consistent with the earliest campaign?
questions.explanation: Forty recorded leaves less the six that belong to the later campaign leaves thirty-four for the earliest one. The sheet should carry both figures so the two campaigns stay distinct.
questions.hint: Remove the later campaign from the recorded total.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Weighing evidence in a disputed attribution
questions.learningObjective: Record an attribution claimed in the press on a defensible costing line

stimulus.body: A short statement issued to the press describes a bronze plaque above a hotel pass as the work of a celebrated sculptor, and the press repeats the claim widely. The statement gives no date, no material analysis and no reference to any document. The kitchen needs to write a defensible line on its costing sheet.

questions.stem: A press statement on the chef's recipe costing sheet names a celebrated sculptor for a bronze plaque and offers no evidence. Which line best fits the sheet?

options.text: Record the plaque as an unknown work, since a claim with no evidence is the same as no claim at all
options.misconception: conflates an unproven claim with the absence of any claim

options.text: Record the plaque as the work of the celebrated sculptor, since wide repetition in the press is itself proof
options.misconception: treats repeated publication as proof of authorship

options.text: Record the claim as an attributed name that remains unverified, and price the plaque on the evidence in hand
Leave the plaque off the sheet entirely, since a named attribution cannot be honoured in a costing
options.misconception: cuts a priced object from the sheet over one doubtful name

questions.explanation: A claim with no evidence can be recorded as a claim, and the plaque priced on what the file shows. Repetition is not proof, an unproven claim is not an absent one, and one doubtful name does not drop the object.
questions.hint: Ask what the file actually shows about the plaque.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a forgery gives itself away
questions.learningObjective: Set out the sound use of three kinds of evidence held in one file
questions.stem: A conservator's file for a panel holds a supplier's invoice, a laboratory report and a stylistic note, and the sheet asks which of the three may be used to fix a date. Which pair of steps best fits the use of that file?

options.text: Choose whichever of the three the kitchen prefers, since the cost sheet sets the outcome
options.misconception: lets the price decide which evidence is used

options.text: Use the invoice as the date, since a document is a document whatever the laboratory found
options.misconception: lets the invoice stand whatever the analysis shows

options.text: Let the stylistic note decide, since style is the one evidence that speaks to the hand directly
options.misconception: assumes style is always the strongest kind of evidence

options.text: Test the laboratory report against the invoice for consistency, then let the stylistic note fill the gap

questions.explanation: The invoice and the laboratory report describe the same object and can be tested against each other, while the stylistic note fills the gap. A document does not survive a contradiction.
questions.hint: Ask which two of the three can be checked against each other.
